claim: CTRP10 protein is highly conserved from zebrafish to human, with an amino acid identity of 67%, 71%, 77%, and 94% between the full-length human protein and the fish, frog, chicken, and mouse orthologs, respectively.
source: CTRP10 protein is highly conserved from zebrafish to human (Figure 1A), with an amino acid identity of 67%, 71%, 77%, and 94% between the full-length human protein and the fish, frog, chicken, and mouse orthologs, respectively.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: The conservation between human and other species CTRP10 orthologs is much higher at the C-terminal globular C1q domain (93–100% identity).
source: The conservation is much higher at the C-terminal globular C1q domain (93–100% identity) between the orthologs.
evidence: Stated in the text based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Among 12 different mouse tissues examined, the brain had the highest expression of Ctrp10.
source: Among the 12 different mouse tissues examined, the brain had the highest expression of Ctrp10 (Figure 1B), consistent with previous findings (Iijima et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by expression data in Figure 1B and cited previous study.

claim: Expression of Ctrp10 in most peripheral tissues was lower than the brain.
source: Expression of Ctrp10 in most peripheral tissues was lower than the brain (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the refed period after an overnight fast, Ctrp10 expression was significantly downregulated in the visceral (gonadal) white adipose tissue (gWAT), liver, skeletal muscle, kidney, cerebellum, cortex, and hypothalamus relative to the fasted state.
source: In the refed period after an overnight fast, we observed a significant downregulation of Ctrp10 in the visceral (gonadal) white adipose tissue (gWAT), liver, skeletal muscle, kidney, cerebellum, cortex, and hypothalamus relative to the fasted state (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by fasting-refeeding experiment data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Male mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks had a modest increase in Ctrp10 expression in brown adipose tissue (BAT) and heart relative to mice fed a control low-fat diet (LFD).
source: Male mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks had a modest increase in Ctrp10 expression in brown adipose tissue (BAT) and heart and decreased expression in skeletal muscle relative to mice fed a control low-fat diet (LFD; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by diet intervention experiment data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Male mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks had decreased Ctrp10 expression in skeletal muscle relative to mice fed a control low-fat diet (LFD).
source: Male mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks had a modest increase in Ctrp10 expression in brown adipose tissue (BAT) and heart and decreased expression in skeletal muscle relative to mice fed a control low-fat diet (LFD; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by diet intervention experiment data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ctrp10 expression is dynamically regulated by acute alterations in energy balance.
source: These data indicate that Ctrp10 expression is dynamically regulated by acute alterations in energy balance, and perhaps to a lesser extent to chronic changes in nutritional state on an obesogenic diet.
evidence: Inferred from the fasting-refeeding and diet intervention experiments described.

claim: The entire protein coding region in exon 1 and 2 of Ctrp10 was deleted using the CRISPR/Cas9 method.
source: The entire protein coding region spanning exon 1 and 2 was deleted. This KO strategy ensures a complete null allele for Ctrp10.
evidence: Stated in the methods and results describing the generation of knockout mice.

claim: The Ctrp10 transcript was absent from KO mice.
source: As expected, based on the gene deletion strategy, the Ctrp10 transcript was absent from KO mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1G confirming complete loss of transcript.

claim: The body weight and body composition of male mice fed a LFD were not different between WT and Ctrp10 KO genotypes.
source: The body weight and body composition of male mice fed a LFD were not different between genotypes (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by body weight and body composition data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: By 20 weeks of age, female KO mice fed LFD had a modestly higher body weight relative to WT controls.
source: By 20 weeks of age, female KO mice fed LFD had a modestly higher body weight relative to WT controls (Figure 2C), although the body composition was not different between genotypes (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by body weight data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The body composition of female KO mice at 13 weeks of age was not different from WT controls.
source: By 20 weeks of age, female KO mice fed LFD had a modestly higher body weight relative to WT controls (Figure 2C), although the body composition was not different between genotypes (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by body composition data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Food intake, physical activity, and energy expenditure were not different between WT and Ctrp10 KO genotypes of either sex across the circadian cycle (light and dark) and metabolic states (ad libitum fed, fasted, refed).
source: Food intake, physical activity, and energy expenditure as measured by indirect calorimetry were also not different between genotypes of either sex across the circadian cycle (light and dark) and metabolic states (ad libitum fed, fasted, refed; Figure 2E–J).
evidence: Supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 2E-J.

claim: No significant differences in fasting and refeeding blood glucose, serum insulin, triglyceride (TG), cholesterol, non-esterified free fatty acids (NEFA), and β-hydroxybutyrate levels were observed between genotypes of either sex, except the female KO mice had slightly lower fasting β-hydroxybutyrate levels.
source: No significant differences in fasting and refeeding blood glucose, serum insulin, triglyceride (TG), cholesterol, non-esterified free fatty acids (NEFA), and β-hydroxybutyrate levels were observed between genotypes of either sex, except the female KO mice had slightly lower fasting β-hydroxybutyrate levels (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by serum metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: No significant differences in glucose and insulin tolerance were noted between WT and Ctrp10 KO genotypes of either sex.
source: No significant differences in glucose and insulin tolerance were noted between genotypes of either sex (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: Supported by glucose and insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: CTRP10 is dispensable for metabolic homeostasis when mice are young (<20 weeks old) and fed a LFD.
source: Together, these data indicate that CTRP10 is dispensable for metabolic homeostasis when mice are young (<20 weeks old) and fed a LFD.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the metabolic phenotyping data of young mice on LFD.

claim: Female KO mice gained significantly more weight and adiposity with age when fed a LFD.
source: Indeed, the female KO mice gained significantly more weight and adiposity with age (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal body weight and body composition data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: By the time the mice reached 40 weeks of age, female KO mice weighed ~6 g (20%) heavier than the WT controls.
source: By the time the mice reached 40 weeks of age, female KO mice weighed ~6 g (20 %) heavier than the WT controls.
evidence: Stated in the text based on body weight measurements over time.

claim: The adipocyte cell size (cross-sectional area) was significantly larger in both gonadal (visceral) white adipose tissue (gWAT) and inguinal (subcutaneous) white adipose tissue (iWAT) of female KO mice.
source: Consistent with greater adiposity, the adipocyte cell size (cross-sectional area) was also significantly larger in both gonadal (visceral) white adipose tissue (gWAT) and inguinal (subcutaneous) white adipose tissue (iWAT) (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Increased weight gain over time in female KO mice was not attributed to differences in food intake.
source: Increased weight gain over time was not attributed to differences in food intake, as measured manually over a 24 hr period (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by manual food intake measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Fecal output, frequency, and energy content were not different between WT and female KO genotypes.
source: Fecal output, frequency, and energy content were also not different between genotypes (Figure 4G), suggesting that weight gain was not due to greater nutrient absorption.
evidence: Supported by fecal analysis data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Deep colon temperatures during both light and dark cycle were not different between WT and female KO genotypes.
source: Deep colon temperatures during both light and dark cycle were also not different between genotypes (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by body temperature measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Indirect calorimetry analyses revealed no significant differences between WT and female KO genotypes in food intake, physical activity, and energy expenditure across the circadian cycle and metabolic states (ad libitum fed, fasted, refed).
source: Indirectly calorimetry analyses also revealed no significant differences between genotypes in food intake, physical activity, and energy expenditure across the circadian cycle and metabolic states (ad libitum fed, fasted, refed; Figure 4I–K).
evidence: Supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 4I-K.

claim: Despite significantly greater body weight and adiposity, female KO mice had the same metabolic profile as the lean WT controls.
source: Despite significantly greater body weight and adiposity, female KO mice had the same metabolic profile as the lean WT controls.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple metabolic assessments showing no differences.

claim: Serum estradiol levels were not significantly different between WT and KO female mice.
source: Given the important role of sex hormone in systemic metabolism, we measured serum estradiol levels and they were not significantly different between WT and KO female mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by estradiol measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no differences in fasting blood glucose, serum insulin, TG, cholesterol, NEFA, and β-hydroxybutyrate levels between WT and female KO genotypes on LFD.
source: There were no differences in fasting blood glucose, serum insulin, TG, cholesterol, NEFA, and β-hydroxybutyrate levels between genotypes (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by serum metabolite measurements shown in Figure 4L.

claim: VLDL-TG levels were lower in female KO mice whereas HDL-cholesterol level was not different between genotypes.
source: Interestingly, VLDL-TG levels were lower in female KO mice whereas HDL-cholesterol level was not different between genotypes (Figure 4M).
evidence: Supported by FPLC lipoprotein analysis shown in Figure 4M.

claim: Direct assessments of glucose handling capacity and insulin sensitivity by glucose and insulin tolerance tests revealed no differences between WT and female KO genotypes on LFD.
source: Direct assessments of glucose handling capacity and insulin sensitivity by glucose and insulin tolerance tests, respectively, also revealed no differences between genotypes (Figure 4N–O).
evidence: Supported by GTT and ITT data shown in Figure 4N-O.

claim: Ctrp10 KO female mice had higher respiration at complex IV relative to WT controls in skeletal muscle.
source: Measurements of mitochondrial respiration in skeletal muscle (gastrocnemius) showed no significant differences in respiration through complex I (CI), CII, and CIV between genotypes; in contrast, Ctrp10 KO female mice had higher respiration at CIV relative to WT controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial respiration measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ctrp10-KO female mice fed LFD develop obesity, but preserve a largely healthy metabolic profile similar to the much leaner WT female mice.
source: Together, these data indicate that Ctrp10-KO female mice fed LFD develop obesity, but preserve a largely healthy metabolic profile similar to the much leaner WT female mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comprehensive metabolic phenotyping of LFD-fed female mice.

claim: When fed a HFD, body weight gain and body composition were not different between WT and Ctrp10 KO genotypes in male mice.
source: When fed a HFD, body weight gain and body composition were not different between genotypes in male mice (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Supported by body weight and body composition data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Food intake, physical activity, and energy expenditure were not different between WT and Ctrp10 KO genotypes in male mice on HFD across the circadian cycle (light and dark) and metabolic states (ad libitum fed, fasted, refed).
source: Food intake, physical activity, and energy expenditure were also not different between genotypes in male mice across the circadian cycle (light and dark) and metabolic states (ad libitum fed, fasted, refed; Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Female KO mice gained weight rapidly on HFD (~9 g or 28% heavier) and had greater adiposity than the WT controls.
source: In striking contrast, female KO mice gained weight rapidly on HFD (~9 g or 28% heavier) and had greater adiposity than the WT controls (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: Supported by body weight and body composition data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: Weight gain in female mice was not due to differences in food intake, body temperature, or changes in fecal output, frequency, and energy content between genotypes.
source: Weight gain in female mice was not due to differences in food intake, body temperature, or changes in fecal output, frequency, and energy content between genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serum estradiol levels were not significantly different between WT and KO female mice on HFD.
source: We measured serum estradiol levels and they were not significantly different between WT and KO female mice on HFD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by estradiol measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Metabolic cage analysis revealed no differences in caloric intake, physical activity, and energy expenditure between WT and KO genotypes in female mice on HFD.
source: Metabolic cage analysis also revealed no differences in caloric intake, physical activity, and energy expenditure between genotypes in female mice (Figure 5I–K).
evidence: Supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 5I-K.

claim: The ANCOVA analysis of energy expenditure using body weight as a covariate did not reveal any differences between WT and KO genotypes in female mice on HFD.
source: The ANCOVA analysis of energy expenditure using body weight as a covariate also did not reveal any differences between genotypes in female mice (Figure 5L).
evidence: Supported by ANCOVA analysis shown in Figure 5L.

claim: The respiratory quotient (RER) was significantly lower in female KO mice relative to WT controls, especially during fasting and refeeding.
source: Interestingly, the respiratory quotient (RER) was significantly lower in female KO mice relative to WT controls, especially during fasting and refeeding (Figure 5M), suggesting a greater reliance on lipid substrates for energy metabolism during those periods.
evidence: Supported by RER measurements shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Hepatic, but not skeletal muscle, mitochondrial respiration through CII and CIV was lower in Ctrp10 KO female mice relative to WT controls on HFD.
source: Interestingly, hepatic, but not skeletal muscle, mitochondrial respiration through CII and CIV was lower in Ctrp10 KO female mice relative to WT controls on HFD (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial respiration measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: CTRP10 is required for female-specific body weight control in response to caloric surplus.
source: Together, these data indicate that CTRP10 is required for female-specific body weight control in response to caloric surplus, but neither food intake, physical activity level, nor whole-body energy expenditure could account for the marked increase in body weight and adiposity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from HFD feeding experiments showing sex-specific effects.

claim: No differences in fasting and refeeding blood glucose, serum insulin, TG, cholesterol, NEFA, and β-hydroxybutyrate levels were noted between genotypes in male mice on HFD.
source: No differences in fasting and refeeding blood glucose, serum insulin, TG, cholesterol, NEFA, and β-hydroxybutyrate levels were noted between genotypes in male mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by serum metabolite measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Female KO mice had higher fasting blood glucose and serum insulin levels compared to the WT controls on HFD.
source: Female KO mice, however, had higher fasting blood glucose and serum insulin levels, and lower β-hydroxybutyrate levels compared to the WT controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by serum metabolite measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Female KO mice had lower fasting β-hydroxybutyrate levels compared to the WT controls on HFD.
source: Female KO mice, however, had higher fasting blood glucose and serum insulin levels, and lower β-hydroxybutyrate levels compared to the WT controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by serum metabolite measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the refed state, serum insulin levels continued to be significantly higher in female KO mice on HFD.
source: In the refed state, serum insulin levels continued to be significantly higher in female KO mice.
evidence: Stated in the text based on fasting-refeeding measurements.

claim: KO female mice appeared unable to suppress serum β-hydroxybutyrate levels in response to refeeding on HFD.
source: Unlike the WT female mice where refeeding markedly lowered serum β-hydroxybutyrate (ketone) levels as expected, KO female mice appeared unable to suppress serum β-hydroxybutyrate levels in response to refeeding (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by fasting-refeeding measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Glucose handling capacity and insulin sensitivity assessments by glucose and insulin tolerance in HFD-fed male mice revealed no differences between WT and KO genotypes.
source: Consistent with the fasting blood glucose and insulin data, glucose handling capacity and insulin sensitivity assessments by glucose and insulin tolerance in HFD-fed male mice also revealed no differences between genotypes (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Supported by GTT and ITT data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: The rate of glucose clearance in response to glucose or insulin injection was virtually identical between WT and KO female mice on HFD.
source: To our surprise, the rate of glucose clearance in response to glucose or insulin injection was virtually identical between WT and KO female mice (Figure 6E–F), suggesting no difference in insulin sensitivity between genotypes.
evidence: Supported by GTT and ITT data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: VLDL-TG and HDL-cholesterol profiles were indistinguishable between WT and KO female mice on HFD.
source: VLDL-TG and HDL-cholesterol profiles were also indistinguishable between WT and KO female mice (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by FPLC lipoprotein analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: CTRP10 is not required for metabolic homeostasis in male mice challenged with a HFD.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that CTRP10 is not required for metabolic homeostasis in male mice challenged with a HFD.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from metabolic phenotyping of HFD-fed male mice.

claim: Loss of CTRP10 markedly promotes weight gain in female mice in the face of caloric surplus, but the excess adiposity is largely uncoupled from obesity-linked insulin resistance and dysregulated glucose and lipid metabolism.
source: In female mice, however, loss of CTRP10 markedly promotes weight gain in the face of caloric surplus, but, paradoxically, the excess adiposity is largely uncoupled from obesity-linked insulin resistance and dysregulated glucose and lipid metabolism.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comprehensive metabolic phenotyping of HFD-fed female mice.

claim: The adipocyte cell size in gonadal (visceral) fat depot of Ctrp10-KO female mice on HFD was significantly larger.
source: Consistent with greater fat mass in visceral (gonadal) fat depot of Ctrp10-KO female mice (Figure 7A), histological analysis and quantification also indicated significantly larger adipocyte cell size (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: The subcutaneous (inguinal) fat pad weight was significantly heavier in female KO mice on HFD.
source: Although the subcutaneous (inguinal) fat pad weight was also significantly heavier in female KO mice (Figure 7C), the adipocyte cell size was marginally bigger but not significant (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by fat pad weight measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The adipocyte cell size in subcutaneous (inguinal) fat depot was marginally bigger but not significant in female KO mice on HFD.
source: Although the subcutaneous (inguinal) fat pad weight was also significantly heavier in female KO mice (Figure 7C), the adipocyte cell size was marginally bigger but not significant (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A bigger fat pad with only marginally larger cell size suggests greater adipocyte hyperplasia in the subcutaneous depot of female KO mice on HFD.
source: A bigger fat pad with only marginally larger cell size suggests greater adipocyte hyperplasia in the subcutaneous depot.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of increased fat pad weight and minimal change in cell size.

claim: Increased adipogenesis in response to caloric surfeit is known to be associated with improved systemic metabolic profile.
source: Increased adipogenesis in response to caloric surfeit is known to be associated with improved systemic metabolic profile (Vishvanath and Gupta, 2019).
evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: The expression of genes associated with inflammation (except for Ccr2), fibrosis, oxidative stress in gWAT and iWAT were not significantly different between female KO mice and WT controls on HFD.
source: Despite marked differences in body weight and adiposity, the expression of genes associated with inflammation (except for Ccr2), fibrosis, oxidative stress in gWAT and iWAT were not significantly different between female KO mice and WT controls (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The expression of some genes associated with ER stress (e.g. Ddit3/CHOP, Atf4, Xbp1) in iWAT were lower in female KO mice on HFD.
source: The expression of some genes associated with ER stress (e.g. Ddit3/CHOP, Atf4, Xbp1) in iWAT were actually lower in female KO mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Quantification of hydroxyproline (marker of fibrosis) and malondialdehyde (marker of oxidative stress) in adipose tissues revealed no significant differences between WT and KO genotypes on HFD.
source: Corroborating the gene expression data, quantification of hydroxyproline (marker of fibrosis), and malondialdehyde (marker of oxidative stress) revealed no significant differences between genotypes (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: Supported by biochemical measurements shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: The liver weight of female KO mice on HFD was modestly increased.
source: The liver weight of female KO mice was modestly increased (Figure 7H), but when normalized to body weight, it was not significantly different from WT controls (2.76% in WT and 2.60% in KO, p=0.24).
evidence: Supported by liver weight measurements shown in Figure 7H.

claim: When normalized to body weight, liver weight was not significantly different between WT and KO female mice on HFD.
source: The liver weight of female KO mice was modestly increased (Figure 7H), but when normalized to body weight, it was not significantly different from WT controls (2.76% in WT and 2.60% in KO, p=0.24).
evidence: Stated in the text based on normalized liver weight calculations.

claim: Histological analysis and quantification revealed no differences in hepatic lipid content (% lipid area) between WT and KO genotypes on HFD.
source: Histological analysis and quantification revealed no differences in hepatic lipid content (% lipid area) between genotypes (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The expression of lipogenic genes (e.g. Fasn) was lower in the liver of female KO mice on HFD.
source: Interestingly, although hepatic fat content was similar between genotypes, the expression of lipogenic genes (e.g. Fasn) was lower and fat catabolism genes (e.g. Cpt2, Ppara, Acadl, Acadm, Acad11, Acadvl) was higher in female KO mice (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The expression of fat catabolism genes (e.g. Cpt2, Ppara, Acadl, Acadm, Acad11, Acadvl) was higher in the liver of female KO mice on HFD.
source: Interestingly, although hepatic fat content was similar between genotypes, the expression of lipogenic genes (e.g. Fasn) was lower and fat catabolism genes (e.g. Cpt2, Ppara, Acadl, Acadm, Acad11, Acadvl) was higher in female KO mice (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The expression of genes associated with inflammation, fibrosis, ER and oxidative stress in liver were not significantly different between WT and KO genotypes on HFD.
source: The expression of genes associated with inflammation, fibrosis, ER and oxidative stress in liver were not significantly different between genotypes (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Quantification of hydroxyproline (marker of fibrosis) in the liver revealed no significant difference between WT and KO genotypes on HFD.
source: Consistent with the gene expression data, quantification of hydroxyproline (marker of fibrosis) in the liver revealed no significant difference between genotypes (Figure 7K).
evidence: Supported by biochemical measurements shown in Figure 7K.

claim: The Ctrp10 KO female mice had higher levels of malondialdehyde (a marker of oxidative stress) in the liver on HFD.
source: The Ctrp10 KO female mice, however, had higher levels of malondialdehyde (a marker of oxidative stress) in the liver, suggesting a modest increase in oxidative stress (Figure 7L).
evidence: Supported by biochemical measurements shown in Figure 7L.

claim: Obesity is largely uncoupled from inflammation, fibrosis, ER, and oxidative stress in Ctrp10 KO female mice on HFD.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that obesity is largely uncoupled from inflammation, fibrosis, ER, and oxidative stress in Ctrp10 KO female mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from gene expression and biochemical analyses of adipose and liver tissues.

claim: Comparison of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) showed robust changes across tissues, with the largest changes seen in the liver of female KO mice on HFD.
source: Comparison of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) via limma (Ritchie et al., 2015) showed robust changes across tissues, with the largest changes seen in the liver (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: In liver, gWAT, and muscle, comparable numbers of DEGs were up- and down-regulated in female KO mice on HFD.
source: In liver, gWAT, and muscle, we observed comparable numbers of DEGs that were up- and down-regulated, whereas more genes were transcriptionally suppressed in the iWAT of Ctrp10 KO female mice (Figure 8E, top panel).
evidence: Supported by DEG analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: More genes were transcriptionally suppressed in the iWAT of Ctrp10 KO female mice on HFD.
source: In liver, gWAT, and muscle, we observed comparable numbers of DEGs that were up- and down-regulated, whereas more genes were transcriptionally suppressed in the iWAT of Ctrp10 KO female mice (Figure 8E, top panel).
evidence: Supported by DEG analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Only limited overlap was observed between the DEGs in each tissue of female KO mice on HFD.
source: While significant DEGs were identified in all four tissues, only limited overlap was observed between the DEGs in each tissue (Figure 8E, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Pathways and processes related to lipid metabolism and estrogen receptor were the top-ranked up-regulated enrichments across tissues in female KO mice on HFD.
source: Pathways and processes related to lipid metabolism and estrogen receptor were the top-ranked up-regulated enrichments across tissues (Figure 8F, top panel), whereas processes related to blood clotting and lipoprotein metabolism were the top-ranked down-regulated enrichments (Figure 8F, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Processes related to blood clotting and lipoprotein metabolism were the top-ranked down-regulated enrichments across tissues in female KO mice on HFD.
source: Pathways and processes related to lipid metabolism and estrogen receptor were the top-ranked up-regulated enrichments across tissues (Figure 8F, top panel), whereas processes related to blood clotting and lipoprotein metabolism were the top-ranked down-regulated enrichments (Figure 8F, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Nr1d1 (also known as Rev-Erbα) is the only gene consistently suppressed across all four tissues (liver, gWAT, iWAT, and muscle) of Ctrp10 KO female mice on HFD.
source: Notably, the nuclear receptor, Nr1d1 (also known as Rev-Erbα), is the only gene consistently suppressed across all four tissues (liver, gWAT, iWAT, and muscle) of Ctrp10 KO female mice (Figure 8E lower panel and Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by DEG analysis shown in Figure 8E and Figure 9.

claim: Global deletion of Nr1d1 promotes lipogenesis, adipose tissue expansion, and obesity.
source: Interestingly, global deletion of Nr1d1 promotes lipogenesis, adipose tissue expansion, and obesity (Delezie et al., 2012; Hand et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: Whole-body and adipose-specific Nr1d1 KO mice fed with HFD become markedly obese, but the obesity is not accompanied by insulin resistance, adipose tissue inflammation, and fibrosis.
source: Although the whole-body and adipose-specific Nr1d1 KO mice fed with HFD become markedly obese, the obesity is not accompanied by insulin resistance, adipose tissue inflammation, and fibrosis (Hand et al., 2015; Hunter et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: HFD-fed mice lacking NR1D1 can maintain a relatively healthy metabolic profile despite being strikingly obese.
source: Like the Ctrp10 KO female mice, HFD-fed mice lacking NR1D1 can maintain a relatively healthy metabolic profile despite being strikingly obese.
evidence: Comparison drawn between Ctrp10 KO and Nr1d1 KO phenotypes based on literature.

claim: In WT mice, NR1D1 acts as a transcriptional repressor of metabolic genes whose expression are upregulated by high-fat feeding.
source: In WT mice, NR1D1 acts as a transcriptional repressor of metabolic genes whose expression are upregulated by high-fat feeding; loss of NR1D1 is thought to result in the de-repression of these genes, leading to greater lipid synthesis and fat mass accrual in response to caloric excess (Hunter et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: Loss of NR1D1 results in the de-repression of metabolic genes, leading to greater lipid synthesis and fat mass accrual in response to caloric excess.
source: In WT mice, NR1D1 acts as a transcriptional repressor of metabolic genes whose expression are upregulated by high-fat feeding; loss of NR1D1 is thought to result in the de-repression of these genes, leading to greater lipid synthesis and fat mass accrual in response to caloric excess (Hunter et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: The suppression of Nr1d1 expression across tissues in HFD-fed Ctrp10 KO female mice may contribute to benign fat mass expansion without the accompanying adipose tissue fibrosis, inflammation, and oxidative stress.
source: Thus, the suppression of Nr1d1 expression—mimicking NR1D1 deficiency—across tissues in HFD-fed Ctrp10 KO female mice may contribute to benign fat mass expansion without the accompanying adipose tissue fibrosis, inflammation, and oxidative stress.
evidence: Inferred from the parallel phenotypes between Ctrp10 KO and Nr1d1 KO mice.

claim: Fgf21 and Fgf1 were significantly elevated in the liver of Ctrp10 KO female mice on HFD.
source: Among the upregulated genes, Fgf21 and Fgf1 were significantly elevated in the liver of Ctrp10 KO female mice (Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 9.

claim: FGF21 is an hepatokine known to improve systemic insulin sensitivity and to promote a favorable metabolic profile in diet-induced obese mice.
source: FGF21 is an hepatokine known to improve systemic insulin sensitivity and to promote a favorable metabolic profile in diet-induced obese mice (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: Hepatic Fgf21 expression is significantly elevated in Ctrp10 KO female mice, but systemic circulating FGF21 levels were only found to be higher (p=0.051) in LFD-fed, but not HFD-fed, KO female mice.
source: While hepatic Fgf21 expression is significantly elevated, its systemic circulating levels were only found to be higher (p=0.051) in LFD-fed, but not HFD-fed, KO female mice (Figure 9—figure supplement 1); this suggests liver-derived FGF21 may be retained and act locally within the liver parenchyma.
evidence: Supported by gene expression and serum FGF21 measurements shown in Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: FGF1 has been shown to dampen hepatic glucose output by suppressing adipose lipolysis.
source: FGF1 is another secreted protein that has been shown to dampen hepatic glucose output by suppressing adipose lipolysis (Sancar et al., 2022), improve systemic insulin sensitivity by reducing adipose inflammation (Zhao et al., 2020), and alleviate hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and insulin resistance (Fan et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: FGF1 improves systemic insulin sensitivity by reducing adipose inflammation.
source: FGF1 is another secreted protein that has been shown to dampen hepatic glucose output by suppressing adipose lipolysis (Sancar et al., 2022), improve systemic insulin sensitivity by reducing adipose inflammation (Zhao et al., 2020), and alleviate hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and insulin resistance (Fan et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: FGF1 alleviates hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and insulin resistance.

evidence: Cited from previous literature.

claim: Upregulated expression of Fgf21 and Fgf1 in Ctrp10 KO female mice could contribute to the MHO phenotype.

claim: The upregulated hepatic expression of IL-22 receptor (Il22ra1) in Ctrp10 KO female mice may confer protection against obesity-associated fatty liver, inflammation and fibrosis.
source: In addition, the upregulated hepatic expression of IL-22 receptor (Il22ra1) in Ctrp10 KO female mice (Figure 9) may confer protection against obesity-associated fatty liver, inflammation and fibrosis (Kong et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: A marked increase in uncoupling protein 3 (Ucp3) and Krüppel-like factor 15 (Klf15) expression in the skeletal muscle may promote lipid utilization and help mitigate lipid-induced insulin resistance in Ctrp10 KO female mice.
source: Further, a marked increase in uncoupling protein 3 (Ucp3) and Krüppel-like factor 15 (Klf15) expression in the skeletal muscle (Figure 9) may promote lipid utilization and help mitigate lipid-induced insulin resistance in Ctrp10 KO female mice (Choi et al., 2007; Fan et al., 2021).
evidence: Inferred from gene expression data and cited literature on UCP3 and KLF15 function.

claim: Combined changes at the level of gene expression and biological pathways and processes across tissues acting in concert likely contribute to the apparently healthy obesity phenotype seen in the KO female mice.
source: Taken together, these combined changes—at the level of gene expression and biological pathways and processes across tissues—acting in concert likely contribute to the apparently healthy obesity phenotype seen in the KO female mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multi-tissue transcriptomic analysis.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of transcriptional correlation of the orthologous DEGs among four metabolic tissues showed differing patterns of gene connectivity between females and males in humans.
source: Hierarchical clustering of transcriptional correlation of the orthologous DEGs among four metabolic tissues—subcutaneous and visceral white adipose tissue, liver, and skeletal muscle—showed differing patterns of gene connectivity between females (Figure 10A) and males (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by GTEx analysis shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: The degree of sex-specific gene correlation pairs of DEGs orthologues showed the most significant differences in subcutaneous adipose tissue in humans.
source: When grouped according to sex in each tissue, the degree of sex-specific gene correlation pairs of DEGs orthologues showed the most significant differences in subcutaneous adipose tissue (Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by GTEx analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Human orthologous genes in subcutaneous adipose tissue and liver exhibited highly significant sex differences in their transcriptional correlation with other DEGs across key metabolic tissues.
source: This analysis showed that human orthologous genes in subcutaneous adipose tissue (Figure 10D, top row) and liver (Figure 10D, third row) also exhibited highly significant sex differences in their transcriptional correlation with other DEGs across key metabolic tissues (Figure 10D).
evidence: Supported by GTEx cross-tissue correlation analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The analyses highlight the sex-specificity of CTRP10 DEG orthologues in humans.
source: These analyses highlight the sex-specificity of CTRP10 DEG orthologues in humans, suggest possible sex-biased mechanisms of tissue crosstalk, and overall underscores the conservation of the sex-dependent metabolic function of CTRP10.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from GTEx analysis of human orthologous genes.

source: Collectively, our findings suggest that CTRP10 negatively regulates body weight in females, and that loss of CTRP10 results in benign obesity with largely preserved insulin sensitivity and metabolic health.
